summary: This standards-track RFC deals with protecting statically provisioned multi-segment pseudowires in MPLS and MPLS-TP at the switching provider edge. Each segment is already protected against tunnel failure, and this adds protection for failure of the S-PE itself. It updates RFC 6870.

plainLanguage.summary: A relay race has runners handing off a baton. If one handoff point fails, this describes how a backup handoff point takes over.

questions: how are static pseudowires protected from s-pe failure
subtitle: How static multi-segment pseudowires survive the failure of a switching router on their path.

tldr.problem: Statically provisioned multi-segment pseudowires are protected against tunnel failure on each segment, but not end-to-end against failure of one of the switching provider edge routers (S-PEs) along the path.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC extends the redundant-pseudowire procedures of RFC 6870 to static pseudowires by using the PW status signaling of RFC 6478 in place of LDP, and it offers an optional alternative based on MPLS-TP Linear Protection.
tldr.outcome: The endpoint T-PEs can switch to a redundant MS-PW when an S-PE fails, as long as both ends are provisioned identically. This RFC updates RFC 6870.

today: RFC 7771 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2016. It updates RFC 6870 and has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC.

sections.title: The Problem: S-PE Failure
sections.content:
In MPLS and MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) networks, pseudowires (PWs) are carried by Label Switched Paths (LSPs), also called tunnels. A Multi-Segment Pseudowire (MS-PW) is a chain: a Terminating Provider Edge router (T-PE) at each end, one or more Switching Provider Edge routers (S-PEs) in between, and a tunneled PW segment joining each neighbouring pair.

Statically provisioned single-segment PWs and each segment of a static MS-PW are already protected against tunnel failure by MPLS-level and MPLS-TP-level tunnel protection. Tunnel protection does not help when an S-PE along the path fails. That gap is what this RFC closes.

The RFC is based on the general PW protection framework in RFC 6718 and on RFC 6870, which describes protection for MS-PWs that are signaled dynamically with LDP. L2TPv3-based PWs are out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: A road already has a spare lane if one bridge breaks. But nobody had planned for what happens if a whole stop in the middle of the trip closes. This document plans for that.

sections.title: Redundant MS-PWs in the Network Model
sections.content:
The RFC reuses the network model from RFC 6718, where a singly homed Customer Edge router (CE) is connected to a T-PE through an Attachment Circuit. In the figure there are three MS-PWs between T-PE1 and T-PE2: PW1 is switched at S-PE1, PW2 at S-PE2 and PW3 at S-PE3.

Having several MS-PWs through different S-PEs gives N:1 protection against S-PE failure for the part of the path from T-PE1 to T-PE2. If the S-PE on the PW in use fails, one of the others can take over.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three different routes from one end to the other, each going through a different middle stop. If one stop closes, you take another route.

sections.title: Extending RFC 6870 to Static Pseudowires
sections.content:
The procedures in RFC 6718 and RFC 6870 rely on LDP-based PW status signaling. It carries the state of the primary MS-PW and the order in which redundant MS-PWs should be used, inside the PW Status TLV.

Static PWs do not use LDP for setup or status. They are provisioned at each T-PE and S-PE by network management systems or other means, and they signal status with the PW OAM message over the PW Associated Channel Header, as defined in RFC 6478. The PW Status TLV carried this way is identical to the LDP one, including the PW Status Codes.

So, for the management of a primary PW and its secondary PWs in Sections 6 and 7 of RFC 6870 to work on static PWs, the status signaling of RFC 6478 MUST be used for the primary and secondary PWs. The endpoint T-PEs then use it in place of LDP, and the RFC 6870 procedures operate identically. The optional S-PE Bypass Mode of RFC 6478 cannot be used, because it requires LDP signaling.
sections.plainLanguage: The two end kids used to talk over one kind of phone line. Static pipes have no such line, so they use a different one that carries exactly the same words.

sections.title: Provisioning Both Ends Identically
sections.content:
Because LDP is not used between the T-PEs of a static MS-PW, the negotiation procedures of RFC 6870 cannot be used. Operators therefore have to take care that the two endpoint T-PEs are identically provisioned.

Specifically, both ends must agree on whether MS-PW redundancy is in use at all. For each protected MS-PW they must also agree on which MS-PW is the primary and on the precedence of the secondary MS-PWs.
sections.plainLanguage: Since the two ends cannot chat to agree on the plan, someone has to give both of them exactly the same written plan beforehand.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 6478 apply to this document. The security considerations of RFC 6718 and RFC 6870 relate to their use of LDP, so they are not required here.

If the alternative approach in the appendix is used, the security considerations of RFC 6378, RFC 7271 and RFC 7324 also apply.
sections.plainLanguage: The safety rules of the phone line the ends use also apply here. If you pick the optional method, you follow its extra safety rules too.

sections.title: Optional Linear Protection Approach
sections.content:
Appendix A offers an OPTIONAL alternative based on MPLS-TP Linear Protection. The Protection State Coordination (PSC) protocol of RFC 6378, RFC 7271 and RFC 7324 was defined for MPLS LSPs only, and the appendix extends it to single-segment and multi-segment PWs. It is useful for end-to-end static MS-PWs over MPLS-TP, where tunnel protection alone cannot protect against S-PE failure.

The protection domain of a point-to-point PW is the two T-PEs and the transport paths between them, a working path and a protection path. PSC treats an SS-PW as a single-hop LSP and an MS-PW as a multiple-hop LSP, so it can also protect against a failed intermediate S-PE. The protected entity does not need to be of the same type as the protecting one, so an SS-PW can be protected by an MS-PW and vice versa.

The Generic Associated Channel (G-ACh) that carries the PSC information is placed in the label stack directly beneath the PW identifier. This approach MUST be identically provisioned at the PE endpoints. For interoperability, all implementations MUST include the approach of the main text even when this alternative is used.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a second, optional way: the two ends keep a main path and a spare path and keep telling each other which one to use. Both ends must be set up the same way.
